body:
Three different hazards

Landslides, snow avalanches and vegetation fires can all threaten settlements, transport routes, forests and human life. However, their physical processes are different. A landslide involves the downslope movement of rock, soil or debris under gravity. A snow avalanche involves the rapid downslope movement of snow, sometimes carrying ice, rocks and other debris. A forest or grassland fire involves the combustion of vegetation and other combustible material.

Understanding the process is essential because the conditions that cause a landslide are not identical to those that cause an avalanche or a forest fire. Similarly, an effective precaution against one hazard may not prevent another.

HazardMain processImportant controlling factors
LandslideGravity-driven movement of soil, rock or debrisSlope, material strength, rainfall, groundwater and ground shaking
Snow avalancheGravity-driven movement of unstable snowSnowpack stability, slope, snowfall, wind and temperature
Forest or grassland fireCombustion and spread through vegetationFuel, ignition, moisture, weather and terrain

Hazard is not the same as disaster risk

A hazard is a potentially damaging physical event or process. Exposure refers to people, buildings, roads or other assets located where that event may occur. Vulnerability describes how susceptible those exposed elements are to harm. Capacity includes the resources and arrangements available to anticipate, withstand and respond to danger.

A steep, unstable hillside may have high landslide susceptibility even when nobody lives below it. Constructing houses or a highway below the same hillside increases exposure. Poor construction, inadequate drainage and limited evacuation access can increase vulnerability. Risk therefore depends on more than the physical hazard alone.

Primary and secondary impacts

A landslide may directly bury a road, but it can also block a river and create a later flood hazard. An avalanche may damage a road or settlement far below the slope where the snow initially broke away. A vegetation fire may cause direct burning, while smoke affects health and subsequent loss of vegetation can increase erosion.

These connections explain why disaster management includes prevention, preparedness, warning, response and recovery rather than attention to the initial event alone.

Prelims focus

  • Landslides and snow avalanches are gravity-driven mass movements.
  • Forest and grassland fires are combustion hazards.
  • Exposure and vulnerability help determine whether a physical hazard becomes a serious disaster risk.
  • Secondary effects may continue after the initiating event.
  • Trap: A highly susceptible location does not necessarily have high human risk if exposure is absent.

[Sources: NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, chapter 5, Geomorphic Processes, section Mass Movements; National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Landslides and Snow Avalanches, June 2009, chapters 1–2.]

title: Understanding Landslides, Snow Avalanches and Vegetation Fires

body:
Gravity and the stability of a slope

A slope remains stable when the forces resisting movement are sufficient to withstand the forces tending to move material downhill. Gravity continuously acts on rock and soil. A landslide occurs when the resistance of a portion of the slope becomes insufficient and that material moves.

Mass movement, also called mass wasting, is the downslope movement of material under the direct influence of gravity. It differs from ordinary erosion, in which an agent such as running water, wind or a glacier removes and transports material. Water may contribute to a landslide without being the agent that carries the entire mass downhill.

Factors that make slopes susceptible

Slope angle and shape

Steeper slopes generally have a stronger downhill component of gravitational force. Cliffs are especially exposed to rockfalls. However, landslides can also occur on gentler slopes when soil is weak, saturated or disturbed. Slope angle is therefore an important factor, not a complete prediction.

Rock and soil characteristics

Loose debris, deeply weathered soil, weak sedimentary layers and fractured rocks may have lower resistance to movement. Joints are fractures in rock, while bedding planes are boundaries between sedimentary layers. If these surfaces provide an unfavourable direction for sliding, a rock mass may move along them.

Weathering can weaken or loosen material and make movement more likely. Nevertheless, weathering is not an essential precondition: comparatively intact rock can also slide or fall along fractures.

Rainfall and groundwater

Heavy or prolonged rainfall is a major landslide trigger. Water enters openings and pores within the slope. Saturation adds weight, while increased pore-water pressure can reduce the effective contact and friction between soil particles or along a potential sliding surface.

Both short periods of intense rain and prolonged rainfall can be dangerous. Prolonged earlier rain may leave a slope saturated before a later storm occurs. A landslide can therefore occur after rain has weakened the slope, even if rainfall at the exact moment of failure is not exceptional.

Seismic activity

Earthquake shaking imposes additional movement and forces on rock and soil. It may dislodge blocks, cause loose material to slide or reactivate an already unstable slope. Landslides are therefore possible during earthquakes even without heavy rainfall.

Vegetation and human disturbance

Plant roots can bind some surface soil, while vegetation cover helps reduce erosion and moderates the movement of water across the ground. Clearing vegetation may weaken this protection, especially on shallow soil slopes. However, trees cannot guarantee stability against deep landslides or large rock movements.

Human activities may increase instability by cutting into the foot of a slope, dumping material near its upper edge, obstructing drainage or excavating without adequate site assessment. A road cutting that removes natural support from the base of a slope is particularly important.

Conditioning factors and triggers

A conditioning factor makes a slope susceptible over time. Examples include weak rock, steep terrain, weathering and unsuitable drainage. A trigger is an event or change that initiates movement, such as intense rainfall, earthquake shaking or removal of support. The distinction is useful because several conditioning factors may exist long before a visible landslide occurs.

A weathered hillside beside a mountain road may remain in place for years. Excavation at its base reduces support, while prolonged monsoon rain raises groundwater pressure. A later heavy shower may trigger the actual movement. The landslide results from interacting factors rather than rainfall alone.

Prelims focus

  • Gravity directly drives mass movement.
  • Rainfall can increase slope loading and pore-water pressure.
  • Earthquakes can trigger landslides without rainfall.
  • Road cuts, overloading and vegetation removal may increase instability.
  • Trap: Weathering assists many landslides but is not necessary for every rockfall or rockslide.

[Sources: NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, chapter 5, Geomorphic Processes, section Mass Movements; NDMA, Management of Landslides and Snow Avalanches, June 2009, chapter 1.]

title: Why Landslides Occur: Slope, Materials, Water and Ground Shaking

body:
Recognising the form of movement

Landslides are not a single uniform process. The material involved and the manner in which it moves help distinguish their main forms. Some movements are relatively coherent slides, while others involve falling or flowing material.

TypeCharacteristic movementKey distinction
Rotational slide or slumpA mass moves along a curved surface.The mass rotates backward relative to the slope.
Debris slideLoose earth and rock debris slide downslope.The movement does not require the backward rotation typical of a slump.
RockslideA rock mass slides along a surface such as a bedding plane, joint or fault.Sliding occurs along an identifiable surface.
RockfallDetached rock blocks fall, bounce or roll from a steep face.Free fall is important; the mass need not remain in contact with a sliding surface.
Debris flowWater-rich soil, rock fragments and other debris move in a flowing mass.The movement behaves more like a dense flow than a coherent slide.

Debris flow should not be confused with ordinary river flow. It contains a large concentration of moving sediment and debris and can travel rapidly through channels. A debris avalanche is a particularly rapid movement of earth material. Despite its name, it is not the same as a snow avalanche.

Major landslide-prone regions of India

The Himalayan belt

The Himalayas are young, tectonically active mountains with many steep slopes, fractured or relatively weak rocks and deposits of unconsolidated material. Earthquake activity, intense rainfall, river erosion and road construction can combine to increase landslide danger. The Himalayan foothills and many mountain roads are therefore important areas for landslide-risk management.

The northeastern hills

Parts of the northeastern hill regions have steep terrain and receive substantial rainfall. Local rock structure, land use and road excavation also influence instability. The level of risk varies between locations; it should not be assumed that an entire state has identical landslide conditions.

The Western Ghats and Nilgiris

The Western Ghats and Nilgiris are generally more tectonically stable than the Himalayas, but this does not make them landslide-free. Steep escarpments, weathered material and heavy rainfall over short periods can cause rockfalls, debris flows and landslides.

Himalayas: young, tectonically active terrain is a major factor. Western Ghats and Nilgiris: steep slopes and intense rainfall remain important despite greater tectonic stability.

Consequences beyond the failed slope

A moving mass can bury settlements, damage agricultural land, destroy bridges and block highways, railway lines or communications. When debris obstructs a river, water may accumulate upstream. Failure of such an obstruction can release water and debris downstream, causing additional flooding or destruction.

Relevance to Gujarat

Gujarat is not part of India's principal Himalayan landslide belt, and snow-avalanche management is not a normal geographical concern for the state. Nevertheless, mountainous and hilly terrain within Gujarat requires suitable slope assessment. For example, road construction and drainage in the hills around Saputara in the Dangs can be examined using the same general principles of rainfall, slope stability and land-use control. Such an example does not imply that every location there has the same mapped hazard level.

Prelims focus

  • A slump involves movement along a curved surface with backward rotation.
  • A rockslide moves along a sliding surface; a rockfall involves falling rock.
  • Debris flows are water-rich mass movements.
  • Important Indian landslide regions include the Himalayas, northeastern hills, Western Ghats and Nilgiris.
  • Trap: Greater tectonic stability does not eliminate rainfall-induced landslides.

[Sources: NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, chapter 5, Geomorphic Processes, section Landslides; NCERT, India: Physical Environment, Class 11, chapter 6, Natural Hazards and Disasters, sections Landslides and Landslide Vulnerability Zones; Government of Gujarat, District Administration of the Dangs, official district information on Saputara, consulted 2 November 2026.]

title: Types of Landslides, Their Distribution in India and Their Consequences

body:
Why landslide maps are prepared

Landslides are strongly influenced by local terrain. Mapping therefore helps planners identify slopes where additional investigation or restrictions may be needed. However, different maps answer different questions.

AssessmentMain purposeImportant limitation
Landslide inventoryRecords locations and characteristics of known past landslides.Past records may be incomplete.
Susceptibility zonationIdentifies places relatively more likely to experience landslide initiation because of terrain conditions.It does not by itself predict the exact day or hour of failure.
Risk assessmentConsiders potential harm to exposed people, infrastructure and other assets.It requires information about exposure and vulnerability as well as the hazard.
Early warningUses current or forecast conditions to indicate increased near-term danger.Warnings have uncertainty and do not guarantee an exact location or time.

What a susceptibility map considers

A susceptibility assessment may combine slope angle, rock type, geological structures, drainage, vegetation, land use, rainfall characteristics and previous landslide locations. Geographic Information Systems and satellite observations help integrate this information.

Areas may be classified into categories such as low, moderate and high susceptibility. These categories are relative indications of terrain conditions. A map showing high susceptibility is not equivalent to an announcement that a landslide will occur immediately.

National Landslide Susceptibility Mapping

The Geological Survey of India (GSI) is the central geological agency responsible for major national landslide studies and susceptibility mapping. Its National Landslide Susceptibility Mapping (NLSM) programme began during the 2014–15 field season and uses a national mapping scale of 1:50,000.

According to a Government of India parliamentary reply dated 20 August 2025, GSI had completed susceptibility mapping for approximately 4.3 lakh square kilometres of landslide-prone hilly and mountainous areas across parts of 19 states and Union Territories. These figures describe the programme's reported status on that date, not a permanent total or a live landslide count.

The National Landslide Forecasting Centre

GSI's National Landslide Forecasting Centre (NLFC) was inaugurated in Kolkata on 19 July 2024. The Bhusanket web portal and Bhooskhalan mobile application were also launched on that date to support the communication of landslide forecasts and the reporting of landslide information.

Forecasting may combine terrain characteristics, rainfall observations, weather forecasts and information about previous landslides. The India Meteorological Department and other data-producing agencies contribute relevant weather information, while the GSI system develops landslide-related assessments. District and state authorities use available warnings for public precautions and administrative decisions.

Monitoring unstable slopes

Monitoring may include repeated ground observations, rainfall measurements, satellite imagery and instruments that detect changes in slope movement or groundwater. Such information can reveal increasing instability, but not every landslide provides an obvious or measurable warning beforehand.

A susceptibility map is primarily a planning tool. A rainfall-based landslide warning addresses a shorter time period. Neither should be interpreted as a guarantee that every individual slope will behave exactly as forecast.

Prelims focus

  • GSI undertakes national landslide susceptibility studies.
  • NLSM uses the mapping scale 1:50,000.
  • The NLFC was inaugurated in Kolkata on 19 July 2024.
  • Bhusanket is associated with landslide information and forecasting; Bhooskhalan is the related mobile application.
  • The 20 August 2025 government reply reported about 4.3 lakh square kilometres mapped across parts of 19 states and Union Territories.
  • Trap: Susceptibility zonation does not give the exact timing of a landslide.

[Sources: NDMA, Management of Landslides and Snow Avalanches, June 2009, chapter 2, Hazard Zonation Mapping; GSI, National Landslide Susceptibility Mapping programme, official Landslide Hazard portal, consulted 2 November 2026; Ministry of Earth Sciences, parliamentary reply on Mapping of Landslide Prone Areas, 20 August 2025; Ministry of Mines, Press Information Bureau release on inauguration of NLFC, 19 July 2024.]
